issues.title: Wallet identity for `coin` settlement: in scope, or sibling spec?
issues.author: douglasborthwick-crypto
issues.body:
Reading draft -01. The abstract is explicit about scope:

> KYAPay does not aim to define agentic identity in its entirety. Rather, it specifies a standard and extensible JWT profile…

PR #18 ("Add note about not being agent identity") makes the boundary even sharper. I want to raise a question that sits exactly on that boundary, and ask whether the answer belongs in this draft or in a sibling specification.

### Observation

The spec defines four identity-bearing claim groups:

- `hid` — Human Identity, with the `verifier` / `verified` / `verification_id` pattern for delegated KYC.
- `apd` — Agent Platform identity, with the same `verifier` / `verified` / `verification_id` pattern.
- `aid` — Agent Identity, identified by `creation_ip` and `source_ips`.
- `sti` — Settlement Information, with sub-claims for `payment_token`, expiration, CVV, etc.

`stp` is a REQUIRED claim with the enum `coin` or `card`, and the Payment Token Issuer role description says settlement happens "via various schemes (Cards, Banks, Cryptocurrency)."

For `stp: card`, `sti` has a complete schema — payment token, expiration, security code, plus the verifier triple. For `stp: coin`, only `sti.type: "usdc"` is defined; no schema exists for the wallet that signs the on-chain transfer, the chain it lives on, or any verifier reference for it.

When `stp: coin`, the buyer agent's on-chain wallet is the field that determines whether the seller can rely on the settlement. KYC on `hid` does not bind to a wallet — a sanctioned or compromised wallet behind a KYC'd human still settles, and on-chain settlements are non-reversible. The current schema gives implementers nowhere to put this information, which suggests `coin` deployments today are either (a) carrying wallet metadata in private extensions to `sti`, or (b) operating without it.

### Question

Does this belong in scope of the KYAPay profile, or is it intentionally deferred to a sibling specification?

If **in scope**, the existing structural pattern would suggest a sibling claim alongside `hid` / `apd` / `aid` (name TBD), mirroring the `verifier` / `verified` / `verification_id` shape that `hid` and `apd` already use:

```
"<wallet-claim>": {                                       // claim name TBD
  "address": "0x...",                                     // canonical wallet identifier
  "chain": "eip155:1",                                    // CAIP-2 chain id
  "verifier": "https://example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
  "verified": true,
  "verification_id": "..."
}
```

This:

- Mirrors the existing `apd` / `hid` claim shape exactly.
- Stays JWT-native — no nested signed structures, no new envelope.
- Defers wallet verification to an external party using the same delegation model the draft already chose for human KYC and agent platform KYA.
- Keeps the spec's existing scope posture: the token *carries* the verified claim; it does not define how the verification is performed.

If **out of scope**, the existing `apd.verifier` precedent suggests the natural home would be a sibling specification defining the wallet identity claim shape, referenced from KYAPay similarly to how the draft references {{IANA.JWT.Claims}} and {{IANA.MediaTypes}}.

I don't have a strong view on which, but the question seems worth pinning down before the next revision — it affects whether implementations of `stp: coin` continue to fork `sti` privately or wait for a normative answer.

Happy to contribute either direction if useful.

issues.title: Define how a recipient compares the host and path in `tdm`
issues.author: skyfire-ankit
issues.body:
Raised by @carlosmgv02 on #59 (https://github.com/skyfire-xyz/draft-skyfire-oauth-kyapay-token/pull/59#issuecomment-6562045971) and on the OAuth list.

`tdm` can carry a host and a path. Identifying the Target and validation step 6 ask a recipient that hasn't onboarded to the issuer to check at least that `tdm` names its domain, but nothing says how a recipient that checks more compares the host and the path. Where a Target keeps tenants on paths under one host, such as `app.beel.es/api/v1/companies/{id}/...`, a domain-only check accepts a token for any path under the domain.

To be addressed in #59:
- a recipient that checks more than the domain compares the host exactly, and matches the path the way cookie paths match (RFC 6265, Section 5.1.4) after RFC 3986 normalization, so `/api` matches `/api/v1` but not `/apidocs`;
- a domain-only check is stated not to enforce the host or the path, so a Target that needs them checks them itself.

issues.title: Add `auth_time` to `hid`
issues.author: skyfire-ankit
issues.body:
From Rob Zagarella's (@Schemo512) implementer review on the OAuth list (item 4 on amr-values, 16 Sep):
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/Px1NpSn3OV3Dr6sJAiUM_Ar1rOs

Rob pointed out that for an action-scoped token, a relying party wants to know that the authentication method ran for this action, not at an earlier login, and that without `auth_time` the `amr` values are true but undated.

Mike asked (21 Sep) when `auth_time` would matter if it differs from the token's issue time:
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/TUy8Pd7vMorJdzzU9Q9DWknqnKQ

Rob's answer (1 Oct): the human may confirm an action at one time and the token be minted, exchanged or re-issued later. `iat` says when the token was created; only `auth_time` says when the human authenticated, so a recipient with a freshness rule needs it.
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/eXDS11eJuwTHA8gaLWr-1q-QWKQ

`hid` carries `amr` (how the human principal authenticated) but not when. Using #24 proposes that a recipient can ask, through `Accept-KYAPay-Token`, for a confirmation no older than `max_age` seconds, measured from `hid.auth_time`:
https://github.com/skyfire-xyz/draft-skyfire-oauth-using-kyapay-tokens/issues/24

Proposal:

- Add `auth_time` as an OPTIONAL sub-claim of `hid`: the time the human principal last authenticated or confirmed, as a NumericDate, with the same meaning as in OpenID Connect Core.
- Where a token is issued for a specific action, state that `hid.amr` and `hid.auth_time` describe the authentication that authorized that action.

pulls.title: Define the clock skew tolerance that Section 4.1.2 already relies on
pulls.author: skyfire-ankit
pulls.body:
Steps 3 and 4 of JWT Payload Validation both require validation "within the verifier's clock drift tolerance", but no value, floor or ceiling appears anywhere in the document, and the companion specification does not mention clocks at all. The concept is invoked and left entirely to the implementer, so two conformant verifiers will choose different allowances and a token one accepts the other rejects -- indistinguishable, from the sender's side, from an attack.

Adds a Clock Skew subsection and points both steps at it.

The bounds: MUST support at least 5 seconds, so nobody ships zero tolerance; SHOULD NOT exceed 60 seconds, with 30 RECOMMENDED. The ceiling is derived rather than picked -- a captured token is acceptable for its lifetime plus twice the tolerance, so a tolerance near the lifetime doubles the exposure that exp exists to bound. This is deliberately stricter than the 5 minutes common in Kerberos, AWS SigV4 and typical OpenID Connect deployments, because the token lifetimes here are short enough that 5 minutes of slack would dominate them.

Also places the burden on the sender, where it can actually be met: a party generating timestamps can compare the Date header of any response from the recipient against its own clock and correct subsequent timestamps. Skew is detectable at the sender and invisible at the verifier, so correcting there is more effective than asking every verifier to be generous.

pulls.title: Locate the issuer JWK Set via RFC 8414 metadata, not by suffix constr…
pulls.author: skyfire-ankit
pulls.body:
…uction

The iss claim currently says the JWK Set is discovered "via the /.well-known/jwks.json suffix mechanism". Three problems with that:

- It is not the construction RFC 8414 defines, which inserts the well-known segment before the path component rather than appending it. An iss with a path component yields a different URL under each reading.
- jwks.json is not a registered well-known URI under RFC 8615.
- RFC 8414 is never cited, so there is nothing to disambiguate against. Two implementers building from this text will construct two different URLs.

Rather than fix the construction and register a new well-known URI, this reads jwks_uri from the issuer's RFC 8414 authorization server metadata, and forbids constructing the URL from iss at all.

Why this way:

- Nothing to register. /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server already exists.
- The issuers in this ecosystem already serve it -- anything built on a standard OAuth AS does, including Okta, Auth0 and Ory.
- Key rotation stops being welded to the issuer identifier. jwks_uri can point at a CDN or a different host without iss changing.
- It is the same discovery the KYA-to-OAuth flow already performs after a 401, so implementers meet it once rather than twice.
- One well-known path per issuer is a smaller surface than an attacker-influenced constructed path.

Cost: one additional fetch per issuer, cached. For an edge verifier that is a cold-start cost amortised across every subsequent request from that issuer.

Also updates the kid validation step to point at the same mechanism instead of restating it, and adds the missing scheme to the KYA-PAY example's iss value -- "kya-pay.example.org" with no scheme leaves retrieval undefined.

NOTE FOR REVIEW: this changes behaviour for anything that implemented the suffix construction, so it wants a look from the co-authors before merging rather than being treated as editorial.

comments.author: skyfire-ankit
comments.body:
Closing in favour of #46.

This proposed reading `jwks_uri` from the issuer's RFC 8414 OAuth authorization server metadata. That is the wrong document type. A KYA issuer is not an authorization server — an issuer performing only identity attestation has no `token_endpoint` and no grant types — so the general case breaks even where our own deployment happens to fit. It also put an OAuth normative dependency inside a JWT profile, aimed at verifiers (bot managers, CDNs) that have no OAuth machinery and no reason to acquire any.

#46 takes the better route: keep the deployed `<iss>/.well-known/jwks.json` convention, state the construction exactly so two implementers cannot derive different URLs, say plainly that it is a path-relative convention rather than an RFC 8615 well-known URI, and record the migration to a registered KYAPay issuer metadata document as a subsection. Nothing that works today stops working, and the direction is on the record.

pulls.title: Specify issuer key discovery precisely and make it RFC 8615 conformant
pulls.author: skyfire-ankit
pulls.body:
The iss claim says the JWK Set is discovered "via the /.well-known/jwks.json suffix mechanism", which is under-specified in a way that produces different URLs from the same token:

- The construction is not stated. Appending to an iss with a path component is not the same as the construction RFC 8615 defines, which scopes well-known URIs to an origin. Two implementers reading this build two different URLs and one of them 404s.
- Trailing-slash handling is undefined.
- jwks.json is not registered under RFC 8615.
- One example iss has no scheme at all, leaving retrieval undefined.

This makes the mechanism exact and RFC 8615 conformant. iss is now REQUIRED to be an origin as defined in Section 4 of RFC 6454 -- a scheme, a host, and an optional port, with no path, query or fragment component. That one restriction settles the first two problems together: with no path there is nothing to append to but the origin, and no trailing slash to handle.

Adds an Issuer Key Discovery section stating that the JWK Set is located at the well-known URI formed from iss with the URI suffix jwks.json -- the construction in Section 3 of RFC 8615 applied to that origin -- with a worked example. The example iss values are corrected to origins; one had lacked a scheme entirely.

Adds a Well-Known URI Registration section registering the jwks.json suffix in the IANA "Well-Known URIs" registry, so the mechanism is conformant rather than merely conventional.

A closing paragraph records that a future revision may additionally define an issuer metadata document, giving an issuer somewhere to advertise capabilities beyond the location of its keys, such as the identity verification methods it supports. Such a document would supplement the mechanism described here rather than replace it.

Supersedes #45, which proposed reading jwks_uri from RFC 8414 OAuth authorization server metadata. That was the wrong document type: a KYA issuer is not an authorization server -- an issuer performing only identity attestation has no token_endpoint -- and it put an OAuth normative dependency inside a JWT profile, aimed at verifiers (bot managers, CDNs) with no OAuth machinery.

pulls.title: State the identity binding on sub
pulls.author: skyfire-ankit
pulls.body:
The subject identifier already binds the identities a KYAPay token asserts: the human principal (`hid`), the agent platform (`apd`) and the agent (`aid`). Change any one of them and the issuer assigns a new subject, so it is a new token. The specification did not state this, and the `sub` entry left the relationship to the identity claims unstated.

This states the existing behaviour, and adds a short Security Considerations subsection on what the binding gives a recipient.

Three smaller corrections come with it.

`sub` is now described as unique rather than pairwise unique. In OpenID Connect Core Section 8, pairwise means a distinct value per relying party, so that relying parties cannot correlate a subject. That is not the behaviour here, since the subject is stable for a given combination of identities across audiences. The word asserted a privacy property the format does not provide.

The agent name is stated to be unique among the agents of an agent platform at a given issuer. The binding, and the new Security Considerations text, both rely on the agent being identifiable, and `aid.name` is what identifies it. The draft previously described the name only as reflecting the agent's business purpose.

The example comments on `sub` are corrected. They described the subject as an agent account identifier, which does not match the binding.

Two further changes came out of review.

The Payment Token Issuer role described settlement only and said nothing about identity verification, which left the subject binding unsupported for PAY tokens. It now states that the issuer conducts KYC and KYB of the Initiator, since KYAPay does not provide for anonymous payment.

A `verified` claim is now restricted to `true`. **This is a compatibility change.** The previous definition read "True if identity verified, otherwise false", so a token carrying `false` conformed to -02 and does not conform here. An issuer does not issue a token carrying unverified claims, so the value should never have been emitted; a KYA-PAY example in -02 nonetheless asserted `false`, and it is corrected. Recipient behaviour on receiving `false` is specified alongside each claim. No issuer is known to emit it.

No new claim, and no change to how tokens are carried.

comments.body:
I'm one of the founders of BeeL., an invoicing API in Spain, and I've been following this from the side of a Target that might receive agent traffic. One gap on path-based tenants.

The PSL rule handles subdomain tenants well. tdm also allows a path, but step 6 only asks a non-onboarded recipient to check that tdm names its domain, and nothing says how the path is compared. Our case: the API is at app.beel.es/api, same host as the web app, with the customer company in the path (app.beel.es/api/v1/companies/{id}/...). Please distinguish these rules so recipients do not use `sub` as a principal-wide correlation or rate-limiting key.

This linkage discussion omits the REQUIRED `aid.name`. Its definition makes `iss`, the agent platform, and the name identify an agent unambiguously, and does not require a different name per Target.
